frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons but remains exposed to European demand, pricing pressure, and competition from alternative suppliers. Energy ties with Italy and broader EU diplomacy are central to preserving leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger creates persistent security and smuggling pressures along Algeria’s southern and eastern borders. Algiers resists external military involvement while expanding surveillance and border controls.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola is reducing dependence on Chinese oil-backed lending, but major infrastructure and debt relationships still constrain fiscal and strategic autonomy. Oil revenues remain vulnerable to external price cycles and trading intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Transit Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S. and European financing to connect Angola with copper and cobalt producers in the interior. The investment improves infrastructure but could intensify competition over transit revenues, concessions, and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and wider Sahel instability threaten trade routes linking Cotonou to landlocked markets. Border closures, sanctions legacies, and militant spillover complicate Benin’s role as a regional logistics hub.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization and transport investment rely heavily on foreign capital and contractors, including Chinese participation. This expands capacity while limiting domestic control over financing terms and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and local beneficiation in its diamond partnership with De Beers. The dispute is commercially manageable but affects government revenue, employment, and long-term control of the diamond value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on diamonds leaves Botswana exposed to global demand shifts and synthetic-stone competition. Efforts to develop copper, critical minerals, and downstream processing are constrained by infrastructure and market scale.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta’s deepening security relationship with Russia reduces Western influence but creates dependence on an external military partner. Limited transparency around security agreements and operating arrangements complicates accountability over national resources.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector and Territorial Control
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state control over gold production and mining revenues, but insecurity limits effective oversight across key producing areas. Artisanal mining, illicit trading networks, and contested territory continue to drain public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: The government is tightening oversight of nickel, gold, and rare-earth projects, but limited technical capacity and opaque contracting leave room for foreign firms and intermediaries to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border tension
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border militant activity and diplomatic tensions with Rwanda constrain trade routes and increase reliance on external security and humanitarian partners.

frictionVectors.title: External port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, tourism, and digital infrastructure rely heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing, creating long-term leverage despite strong national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde retains formal control over its maritime zone, but limited patrol capacity leaves fisheries protection and anti-trafficking operations dependent on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, timber, mining, and infrastructure concessions remain vulnerable to elite brokerage and foreign commercial influence, limiting transparent domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-zone infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies in the Far North and Anglophone regions disrupt roads, energy projects, and agricultural supply chains while increasing dependence on external security and humanitarian support.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-resource nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and associated commercial networks remain central to regime protection, with mining access and preferential concessions reinforcing asymmetric external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on neighboring states and foreign-backed corridors for fuel, trade, and humanitarian access, leaving sovereignty highly exposed to regional conflict and border closures.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the fiscal backbone, but foreign operators, export infrastructure, and opaque revenue management constrain the state's effective control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Competing security patrons
frictionVectors.details: Chad balances French, Western, Gulf, and increasingly Russian-linked security relationships while instability in Sudan and the Central African Republic raises pressure on its borders and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: French Territorial Control
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, making sovereignty and maritime-boundary claims a persistent diplomatic issue for Moroni. The dispute limits Comoros's effective control over surrounding waters and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on foreign financing and contractors. This improves access but leaves the country vulnerable to outside leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals remain dominated by foreign firms and opaque state-linked arrangements. Kinshasa is seeking greater value retention, but weak governance and limited processing capacity constrain sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Linked Conflict
frictionVectors.details: M23 activity and regional military tensions continue to threaten territorial control in eastern Congo. Conflict also disrupts mining corridors and creates openings for illicit cross-border resource flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and export earnings remain heavily tied to oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price volatility and foreign operating partners. Limited diversification reduces bargaining power over the broader resource economy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing provide roads, ports, and urban projects but increase dependence on external capital. Debt servicing and project control can narrow the government's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Concentration
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors remain central to ports, telecoms, energy, and agro-processing. Abidjan is improving local value capture, but strategic infrastructure remains substantially externally financed.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and producer regulation, yet foreign traders and manufacturers still capture much of the cocoa value chain. Climate stress and farmer incomes add pressure to this model.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and diplomatic leverage but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy. Rivalry among external powers raises the value and risk of its territory.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and financing, particularly involving China, have increased Djibouti's role in regional trade while creating debt and control concerns. Competition with alternatives in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa makes revenues vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Suez and Red Sea Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and rerouting around the Red Sea continue to threaten Suez Canal revenues and Egypt's external financing. Cairo is balancing maritime security cooperation with the need to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Egypt's central water-security concern. Diplomatic pressure is constrained by regional rivalries and limited appetite for military escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output is narrowing fiscal space and increasing dependence on foreign operators, technical partners, and new offshore investment. Malabo is seeking gas monetization while retaining tight political control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign involvement in ports, logistics, and energy infrastructure gives external partners influence over the country's declining resource base. Limited transparency complicates assessment of sovereign returns and debt exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing interest from Gulf states and other regional powers. Asmara seeks leverage without accepting durable foreign basing arrangements that could dilute its autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Partnerships and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide scarce foreign exchange but remain vulnerable to governance criticism, labor concerns, and dependence on foreign technical and financial partners. This limits the state's ability to capture the full value of its mineral assets.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's access to ports, electricity, finance, and regional supply chains remains heavily dependent on South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This constrains independent resource and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Diplomatic Recognition Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Taiwan provide development and technical support but expose Mbabane to pressure from China and wider regional diplomatic trends. The partnership remains useful, though its long-term sustainability is uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over its hydropower future but remains a major source of friction with Egypt and Sudan. Disputes over operating rules and drought management continue to carry escalation risk.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring and Foreign Finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressure and the need for external financing give China, Gulf investors, and international financial institutions greater influence over infrastructure and macroeconomic policy. Conflict-related instability further weakens the state's bargaining position.

highlights: Transition seeks greater control over oil and manganese
France recalibrates as China expands commercial reach

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for more domestic value capture and tighter oversight of foreign concessions. This may generate friction with established French, U.S., and Chinese operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export infrastructure remains dependent on foreign capital and operators, particularly for manganese and other bulk commodities. Chinese financing and Gulf commercial interest are increasing their leverage.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty remains tied to external finance
Senegal is the decisive security and trade partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese strategic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for security coordination, transport access, and regional trade. This limits policy autonomy despite broadly cooperative relations.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak enforcement threaten local livelihoods and food security. Tourism, port, and energy projects also leave the country dependent on outside investors and donors.

highlights: Gold remains powerful, but illegal mining erodes state control

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining, environmental damage, and illicit gold flows reduce public revenue and weaken state control over a strategic asset. Foreign equipment, financiers, and trading networks complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms limit fiscal room and shape energy, taxation, and public-investment choices. Ghana retains policy capacity, but external financing remains a major constraint.

highlights: Bauxite power is shifting toward Simandou’s iron ore boom
Junta-led nationalism meets deep Chinese infrastructure dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou concession politics
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou project could transform state revenues but gives foreign consortiums major influence over mines, railways, and ports. Contract terms, local processing, and revenue distribution remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea depends heavily on foreign firms and Chinese-linked infrastructure to export bauxite. The government is seeking more domestic value addition while risking investor and regional transport friction.

highlights: Cashew exports provide revenue but little processing power

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing. Infrastructure and finance constraints reinforce this pattern.

frictionVectors.title: Security and trafficking networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and political instability create openings for transnational drug trafficking and external patronage. Regional security dependence, especially involving Senegal and wider West African partners, narrows autonomous decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Financing
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing around Mombasa port and transport corridors. Debt-servicing pressure limits Nairobi's room to renegotiate infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Positioning
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms are seeking access to Kenya's emerging mineral prospects, while Nairobi is trying to strengthen local processing and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose the kingdom to disputes over tariffs, construction delays, and ecological costs.

frictionVectors.title: External Mining and Manufacturing Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign ownership remains dominant in diamonds and export-oriented textiles, leaving employment and fiscal stability vulnerable to external market and investment decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large iron ore and gold projects are drawing foreign capital, but Liberia remains challenged to convert concession activity into domestic processing, reliable tax receipts, and broad-based employment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financiers retain significant influence over ports, rail links, and export corridors, constraining Monrovia's control of strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over fields, export terminals, and budget flows, weakening the National Oil Corporation's ability to act as a unified sovereign instrument.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors pursue overlapping security and energy interests, embedding foreign leverage in Libya's infrastructure and political settlement.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and graphite projects provide investment and exports but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, environmental disputes, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Concessions
frictionVectors.details: External operators and financiers are increasingly important to mining corridors and port infrastructure, raising concerns over tariff control, strategic access, and national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-Linked Fiscal Austerity
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions constrain domestic policy space, while foreign-exchange shortages limit Malawi’s ability to secure fuel, fertilizer, and industrial inputs.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects depend heavily on external capital and transport corridors, raising concerns over value capture, energy access, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state shares and revised terms, increasing legal and operational uncertainty around major gold assets.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel provides regime support but deepens external influence and complicates Western sanctions, investment, and oversight of resource zones.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers major fiscal upside but requires durable bilateral arrangements on revenue sharing, local content, and maritime security.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and emerging gas production remain dependent on foreign operators, concessional finance, and port-rail infrastructure, limiting near-term domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Transition Risks
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty transition over the Chagos Archipelago, including Diego Garcia, requires careful management of security, basing, and maritime-resource arrangements with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius remains highly dependent on imported fuel, food, and technology, leaving its economy vulnerable to shipping disruptions and external price shocks despite strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Morocco’s control and investment in Western Sahara remain contested, creating diplomatic, legal, and reputational risks around fisheries, phosphates, renewable energy, and infrastructure projects.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Stress
frictionVectors.details: Severe water scarcity and dependence on imported hydrocarbons pressure Morocco’s sovereignty over food and energy systems, even as it expands renewables, desalination, and green-hydrogen capacity.

highlights: Port and Gas Corridors Draw External Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security
frictionVectors.details: Persistent militant activity continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and delay the full return of major foreign energy projects. Mozambique remains dependent on external security assistance while seeking greater control over offshore gas revenues.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy firms, Gulf investors, and international lenders retain substantial influence over gas, logistics, and export infrastructure. Local-content gains have not yet translated into decisive sovereign control.

highlights: Oil and Uranium Capital Inflows Intensify

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen and Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: International firms and development partners are financing major hydrogen and petroleum projects, creating jobs and infrastructure while raising concerns over fiscal terms, domestic value capture, and long-term export dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large industrial projects could intensify pressure on scarce water and electricity supplies. Namibia is pursuing local processing and renewable capacity, but infrastructure expansion remains vulnerable to external finance and technology dependence.

highlights: Oil Export Route Tests Regional Autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Dispute with France
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are pressing to renegotiate or end longstanding French influence over uranium assets, but production, financing, and technical operations remain constrained by the confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's oil exports depend heavily on the cross-border pipeline to Benin, making commercial revenue vulnerable to diplomatic tensions, sanctions exposure, and insecurity along transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Vandalism, theft, and insecurity in the Niger Delta continue to reduce public revenue and weaken federal control over strategic energy infrastructure. Security partnerships and foreign operators remain central to maintaining production.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western capital is important for ports, rail, power, and hydrocarbons. Domestic refining capacity improves leverage, but debt, currency pressure, and imported technology limit full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained international scrutiny over alleged support to armed actors and the movement of minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Diplomatic pressure threatens trade access and complicates Kigali's effort to position itself as a responsible mineral-processing hub.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over strategic policy, but its development model depends on foreign aid, investment, and security relationships. Tensions with Western partners could narrow fiscal and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing pressure
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms continue to show interest in São Tomé and Príncipe's offshore blocks, but weak commercial discoveries and limited state capacity constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on external partners for ports, power, telecoms, and development finance, creating vulnerability to shifting Portuguese, Chinese, and Gulf interests.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Dakar greater fiscal leverage, but contract reviews and local-content demands risk tension with international operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing access and coastal security
frictionVectors.details: Industrial foreign fishing and maritime overcapacity continue to pressure artisanal livelihoods, while Senegal seeks stronger control over its fisheries and offshore infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from Indian Ocean maritime-security partnerships, but expanded Indian, European, and other external activity requires careful protection of strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and marine-resource dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on tourism and imported infrastructure leaves the islands exposed to external finance, climate shocks, and pressure over access to maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and rutile leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining capital remains central to export earnings, while disputes over taxation, local benefits, environmental impacts, and concession terms limit domestic control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Freetown logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, road, and energy upgrades depend substantially on external finance and operators, creating long-term exposure to creditor and investor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: External security architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is expanding control over its waters and security institutions, but remains dependent on foreign military assistance, training, and financing while confronting al-Shabaab.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-access rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and other interests in ports and maritime access give Mogadishu leverage but also intensify sovereignty disputes and federal-regional tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Investment Competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is using its critical-minerals base to attract processing and industrial investment, but competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf interests limit Pretoria's room to impose stricter local-beneficiation terms.

frictionVectors.title: Eskom and Freight Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity unreliability and deteriorating freight rail and port capacity weaken sovereign control over mining exports and increase dependence on private and foreign infrastructure capital.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production, revenue, and market access vulnerable to external leverage and transit disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and External Resource Capture
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation, armed-group financing, and opaque oil contracting constrain public control over hydrocarbons while neighboring states and foreign commercial actors compete for access.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Wartime Finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade remain central to financing rival wartime networks, with foreign buyers and intermediaries benefiting from weak state oversight and fragmented territorial control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Control over Port Sudan, Red Sea access, and humanitarian and commercial corridors has become a strategic contest involving regional powers and external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Negotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger state participation and domestic benefits from offshore gas development, but project financing and export infrastructure give international energy firms substantial negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Transport Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades to Dar es Salaam's port, rail, and regional corridors are attracting Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western interest, creating opportunities while increasing exposure to external infrastructure influence.

frictionVectors.title: Port Dependency and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and logistics economy provide strategic revenue, but reliance on foreign operators, lenders, and shipping networks limits the state's control over critical trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel is forcing greater security spending and external cooperation, while instability threatens transport corridors linking Togo to landlocked neighbors.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial and diplomatic support remains tied to migration control, giving external partners significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic criticism centers on sovereignty and accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains reliant on imported energy and vulnerable to fiscal pressure from subsidies and supply disruptions. Delayed renewable investment limits near-term autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental opposition
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated fields remain central to Uganda's resource strategy but face international legal, activist, and reputational pressure. Chinese and Gulf-linked financing help sustain the project while increasing external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects have expanded connectivity but increased obligations to foreign lenders and contractors. Kampala retains policy autonomy, though repayment pressures narrow fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to seek better terms in copper and cobalt. Processing capacity and ownership remain more externally controlled than Lusaka's political messaging suggests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor restructuring have stabilized access to finance but constrain spending and industrial-policy choices. Improved fiscal credibility has not yet translated into full control of mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mining operations, while Western and regional investors retain influence in finance and technology. Export restrictions have encouraged beneficiation but enforcement and local capacity remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Financial isolation and currency stress
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted capital access, and persistent monetary instability weaken the state's bargaining position with external investors. Reliance on mineral receipts and informal channels limits effective sovereign control over revenue.
